'''''Lysimachia vulgaris''''', the  '''yellow loosestrife''' or '''garden loosestrife''', is a species of [[herbaceous]] [[perennial]] [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Primulaceae]]. It was transferred to [[Myrsinoideae]] based on results of molecular [[Phylogenetics|phylogenetic research]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hao |first1=Gang |last2=Yuan |first2=Yong-Ming |last3=Hu |first3=Chi-Ming |last4=Ge |first4=Xue-Jun |last5=Zhao |first5=Nan-Xian |title=Molecular phylogeny of ''Lysimachia'' (Myrsinaceae) based on chloroplast ''trn''L–F and nuclear ribosomal ITS sequences |journal=Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution |date=2004 |volume=31 |issue=1 |pages=323–339 |doi=10.1016/S1055-7903(03)00286-0}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Oh |first1=Il-Chan |last2=Anderberg |first2=A.-L. |last3=Schönenberger |first3=J. |last4=Anderberg |first4=A. A. |title=Comparative seed morphology and character evolution in the genus ''Lysimachia'' (Myrsinaceae) and related taxa |journal=Plant Systematics and Evolution |date=2008 |volume=271 |issue=3-4 |pages=177–197 |doi=10.1007/s00606-007-0625-z |jstor=23657317 }}</ref> before being merged into the Primulaceae.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Angiosperm Phylogeny Group |title=An update of the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group classification for the orders and families of flowering plants: APG III |journal=Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society |date=2009 |volume=161 |issue=2 |pages=105–121 |doi=10.1111/j.1095-8339.2009.00996.x}}</ref>

==Description==
Yellow loosestrife is a tall downy semi-evergreen perennial plant with an upright habit, {{cvt|50–150|cm}} high, with erect panicles of conspicuous yellow flowers.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|authorlink = Stace, C. A.|year=2010|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Third|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location = Cambridge, U.K.| isbn=9780521707725}}</ref>{{rp|519}} The edges of the petals lack the fringe of hairs seen in ''[[Lysimachia punctata|L. punctata]]'', and the hairy, narrow triangular sepals have a conspicuous orange margin.<ref name=Blamey>{{cite book|last1=Blamey|first1=M.|last2=Fitter|first2=R.|last3=Fitter|first3=A|year=2003|title=Wild flowers of Britain and Ireland: The Complete Guide to the British and Irish Flora |publisher=A & C Black|location=London|isbn=978-1408179505}}</ref>{{rp|114}} It flowers from June through August in the British Isles. Measuring {{cvt|5-12|cm}} long, the entire-margined leaves are opposite or 3–4-whorled, ovate to lanceolate and spotted with translucent orange glands.

The stem is round or square in cross-section, downy, and usually solid and pith-filled<ref>Poland J, Clement EJ. 2020. ''The Vegetative Key to the British Flora''. John Poland, Southampton {{ISBN|9780956014429}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The generic name ''Lysimachia'' means ‘ending strife’, derived from [[Lysimachus]], a King of [[Thrace]], [[Asia Minor]] and [[Macedon]], also an army leader under [[Alexander the Great]]. The [[specific epithet]] ''vulgaris'' means common, or usual.<ref>Gledhill D. 1985. The Names of Plants. Cambridge University Press {{ISBN|0521366755}}</ref>

==Habitat, distribution and ecology==
''L. vulgaris'' is native to [[Eurasia]], as far West as [[Ireland]] where it is frequent to locally common, and North Africa. It has been introduced to North America, where it is considered an exotic introduction, for its ornamental value in gardens. It grows best in moist habitats such as fens and wet woodlands as well as on lakesides and riverbanks.

Like many of its [[Congener (biology)|congeners]], ''L. vulgaris'' provides an important [[nectar]] source for specialist [[solitary bees]] in the genus ''[[Macropis]]'', especially ''[[Macropis europaea]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Garbuzov |first1=Mihail |last2=Ratnieks |first2=Francis L. W. |title=Listmania: The strengths and weaknesses of lists of garden plants to help pollinators |journal=BioScience |date=2014 |volume=64 |issue=11 |pages=1019–1026 |doi=10.1093/biosci/biu150}}</ref> However, the relationship between ''Lysimachia'' and ''Macropis'' is not thought to be obligate on the part of the plant.<ref>Popov VV. 1958. Special features of the correlated evolution of ''Macropsis epeloides'' (Hymenoptera, Apoidea) and ''Lysimachia'' (Primulaceae). ''Entomological Reviews'' 37: 433–451</ref>

For the first time, a plant pathogen ''[[Ramularia|Ramularia lysimachiae]]'' was found on the plant in [[County Durham]] in 2004.<ref>Legg AW. 2004. ''Ramularia lysimachiae'' Thüm on ''Lysimachia vulgaris'' - a new plant-fungus association for Great Britain, found in County Durham. ''Vasculum'' 89(3)</ref>

''L. vulgaris'' has been listed as a [[noxious weed]] in [[Washington (state)|Washington State]] and [[Oregon]] on account of its invasiveness. Although the seeds only appear to have a maximum viability of 3 years when stored in the soil, the plant can spread by vegetative means from [[rhizomes]] over extensive areas, sometimes to the detriment of other species.<ref>DiTomaso JM, Kyser GB, Oneto SR, Wilson RG, Orloff SB, Anderson LW, Wright SD, Roncoroni, JA, Miller TL, Prather TS, Ransom C. 2013. Weed control in natural areas in the western United States. ''Weed Research and Information Center, University of California'', 544.</ref> It remains in a vegetative state for some years before blooming, so that flowering stands of the plant indicate that it has long been present in that area.<ref>Cusick AW. 1986. Distributional and taxonomic notes on the vascular flora of West Virginia. ''Castanea'' 51 (1): 56–65.</ref>

''L. vulgaris'' is an unpalatable species that is avoided by large herbivores due to its content of toxic compounds.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bossuyt |first1=B. |last2=de Fré |first2=B. |last3=Hoffmann |first3=M. |title=Abundance and flowering success patterns in a short‐term grazed grassland: early evidence of facilitation |journal=Journal of Ecology |date=2005 |volume=93 |issue=6 |pages=1104–1114 |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2745.2005.01059.x}}</ref>

==In use==
Like many other plants in the genus ''Lysimachia'', yellow loosestrife has historically been valued for its medicinal properties and is still sometimes used today in traditional folk medicine by some eastern cultures. It has been used as an effective anti-inflammatory agent as well as for treating fever, wounds, ulcers, and diarrhoea.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Podolak |first1=I. |last2=Elas |first2=M. |last3=Cieszka |first3=K. |title=''In vitro'' antifungal and cytotoxic activity of triterpene saponosides and quinoid pigments from ''Lysimachia vulgaris'' L. |journal=Phytotherapy Research |date=1998 |volume=12 |issue=S1 |pages=S70–S73 |doi=10.1002/(SICI)1099-1573(1998)12:1+<S70::AID-PTR254>3.0.CO;2-9}}</ref> It also has [[analgesic]], [[astringent]], and [[expectorant]] properties.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yildirim |first1=Arzu Birinci |last2=Guner |first2=Birgul |last3=Karakas |first3=Fatma Pehlivan |last4=Turker |first4=Arzu Ucar |title=Evaluation of antibacterial, antitumor, antioxidant activities and phenolic constituents of field-grown and in-vitro-grown ''Lysimachia vulgaris'' L. |journal=African Journal of Traditional, Complementary and Alternative Medicines |date=2017 |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=177–187 |doi=10.21010/ajtcam.v14i2.19 |pmid=28573234 |pmc=5446442}}</ref>
